analysis.one_liner: Strips the EPA's power to limit greenhouse gas pollution under the Clean Air Act.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced in February 2010 with 17 cosponsors from both parties, it died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the Clean Air Act so that carbon dioxide and five other greenhouse gases no longer count as air pollutants when it comes to climate change. That would remove the EPA's legal authority to set limits on greenhouse gas emissions from power plants, factories, and vehicles. It would also rewrite the federal renewable fuel program so that biofuel makers are not penalized for emissions caused when land is converted to crops overseas, and would widen the definition of which wood and crop materials count as "renewable biomass."
analysis.who_benefits: Major greenhouse gas emitters — coal-fired power plants, oil and gas companies, and energy-intensive manufacturers — would be freed from any federal EPA limit on their carbon emissions, avoiding compliance costs. Biofuel and ethanol producers would gain because their fuel could no longer be downgraded under the renewable fuel standard for land-use emissions tied to growing feedstocks. Forest products and agricultural interests would gain a wider set of materials that count as "renewable biomass."
analysis.who_benefits_short: Power plants, oil companies, and biofuel makers

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds greenhouse gases to the list of things that cannot be treated as air pollutants "solely on the basis" of their effect on climate, which would bar the EPA from using its Clean Air Act authority to limit carbon dioxide, methane, and related emissions. [S2] [S3]

It forbids the EPA from considering indirect emissions from international land-use changes when implementing the renewable fuel program, sparing biofuel producers from having their fuels penalized for deforestation linked to crop expansion abroad. [S2] [S3]

It redefines "renewable biomass" to include forest thinnings and invasive species removed from national forests and any organic matter from non-federal land — including feed grains, crop residue, and animal waste — expanding the supply of materials that qualify for renewable fuel credit. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: If the bill had passed, ordinary people would bear the costs of unchecked greenhouse gas emissions — heat waves, storms, and other climate impacts — with no federal program to limit them. The accounting change in the renewable fuel standard would also let the climate damage of land conversion abroad go uncounted when federal policy steers billions of gallons of fuel choices.

drawbacks.text: Removing greenhouse gases from the Clean Air Act's definition of air pollutants would leave no federal regulator with the power to limit carbon pollution, since the EPA's authority is the foundation of U.S. climate policy under that statute. [S2] [S3]

The biofuel provisions change how emissions are counted rather than how much fuel emits: excluding international land-use change from "lifecycle" emissions makes biofuels look cleaner on paper without changing real-world emissions, and shifting part of the calculation to the Agriculture Department moves the science further toward the industry it supports. [S2] [S3]

The strongest good-faith argument for the bill is that unelected regulators at the EPA were poised to impose sweeping climate rules after the courts authorized it, and that Congress — not an agency — should set such consequential policy; an honest supporter would acknowledge that the bill offered no substitute policy, only removal of the existing one.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow to identifiable industries — big emitters and biofuel producers — in the form of avoided regulation and easier accounting. Its costs are diffuse and long-term: unmeasured and unregulated climate pollution borne by the public. Because it removes regulatory authority without replacing it with any policy of its own, the cost side clearly outweighs the benefit side for ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2010 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then its energy subcommittee, which never held a markup or vote, so it died when that Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Ike Skelton, a Missouri Democrat, introduced the bill on February 2, 2010, joined by Reps. Collin Peterson and Jo Ann Emerson, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce. [S1] [S5]
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Environment, and no further action was ever taken on it. [S5]

Seventeen members cosponsored the bill — 5 Democrats and 12 Republicans — but the committee never scheduled a hearing or markup and the full House never voted on it before the 111th Congress ended. [S4] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the EPA kept its Clean Air Act authority over greenhouse gases and major emitters did not get the exemption they sought. Biofuel producers also did not get the land-use accounting relief they wanted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ordinary people; major emitters gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Ike Skelton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip the EPA's authority over greenhouse gases and rewrite the renewable fuel standard

for.name: Rep. Collin Peterson
for.what_they_did: Joined in introducing the bill, which carried the biofuel and biomass provisions central to farm-district interests

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral for Clean Air Act legislation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — letting it die in committee

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but lopsided in style, not numbers: a Missouri Democrat and the Democratic Agriculture chairman led it, with 5 Democrats and 12 Republicans among the 17 cosponsors; neither party's leadership moved it.

industries.industry: Coal-fired power plants and other major greenhouse gas emitters
industries.note: The bill would have barred the EPA from limiting their carbon dioxide and methane emissions under the Clean Air Act, eliminating compliance costs. The public would bear the resulting pollution and climate damage in exchange.

The bill would have exempted them from land-use-change penalties in the renewable fuel standard and expanded which biomass counts as renewable, raising the value of their product and the federal mandate behind it. Biofuels also serve a public low-carbon goal, but the change works by counting fewer emissions, not emitting less.

A wider definition of "renewable biomass" would let them sell forest thinnings, crop residue, and waste materials as qualifying renewable fuel feedstock, creating a new revenue stream from materials now left in the field or woods.
